title: Pauri 10: listening, truth and contentment
hookLine: suniai: by listening come truth, contentment and wisdom, worth bathing at every shrine (Japji 10)
tomorrow: Pauri 11: listening, the blind find the way

cards: You're scrolling past a jacket, a phone, a trip, and you already have one that works perfectly well. Still there's a little tug: but this one's better. The tug never quite goes away; there's always a next one.
Then there are the rare moments it stops. A meal with friends where nobody checks the time. A quiet evening when nothing is missing.
Pauri ten has a name for that feeling, and says where it comes from.

teach.b: Here is pauri ten in plain words, following Macauliffe. By listening come truth, contentment and divine knowledge. By listening, the bath at the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage.
By listening, reading and reading, honor is won. By listening, the mind settles easily into meditation. Nanak, the devotees are always in bloom.
By listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away.
The heart of it is the first line: suniai sat santokh giaan. Sat is truth, the same root as sach. Giaan is knowledge, wisdom.
And in the middle, today's word: santokh. Contentment. Enough.

Not giving up, not pretending not to want anything: the settled feeling of having enough, the tug gone quiet. Sikh teaching often counts santokh among the great virtues, alongside truth, compassion, humility and love.
And the pauri says it comes from listening. Not from getting the next thing, and not from grimly denying yourself, but from hearing the Name until the restless wanting loosens its grip on its own.

Then the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage. Indian tradition counted sixty-eight great bathing places, and people walked for months to reach them. Pauri six said the bath is only worth it if it pleases Him.
Here Guru Nanak says it plainly: listening is the bath at all sixty-eight at once. And last before the refrain: sahaj dhiaan.
Sahaj is ease, naturalness: the meditation that comes without forcing.
You don't have to wrestle the tug down. You listen, and it quiets.

how: Sikhs recite the tenth pauri each morning; santokh, contentment, is often taught as one of five virtues, with sat (truth), daya (compassion), nimrata (humility) and pyaar (love).

o: a holy bath at a place of pilgrimage
giving up all wanting by sheer force
contentment, the settled sense of enough

games.q: what's inside the pauri — tap the pairs.

s: santokh means giving up all wanting by force
it's the settled sense of enough, which comes by listening, not by grim denial.
the pauri says listening is worth a bath at sixty-eight shrines
santokh is counted among the great Sikh virtues
with truth, compassion, humility and love.

games.q: you want contentment, the feeling of enough. where does pauri ten say it comes from?
games.why: suniai sat santokh giaan: by listening come truth, contentment and wisdom, and listening is itself the bath at all sixty-eight shrines.

practice: Pick one thing exactly as it is: your chair, your hands, the light in the room, this day so far.

Don't improve it or compare it to a better version; just let it be enough, and when the tug comes, notice it and go back to listening, to your breath, to the room. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Santokh. Contentment, the settled sense of enough. Japji's tenth pauri says it comes by listening.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: santokh, contentment. from pauri 10: ਸੁਣਿਐ ਸਤੁ ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਗਿਆਨੁ.

carryVoice: Your line: enough, by listening. Contentment and ease, and neither one forced. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 10
